findings.title: ADR-0016 Case B wrapper command can bypass user permissions.deny because the deny matcher never sees the real command
findings.claim: Case B rewrites a denied Bash call into `node <bundle>/run.mjs <base64 of the original command>`, which the subagent then runs itself with Bash.
findings.evidence: ADR-0016 'Three cases' table, Case B: 'The command becomes node <bundle>/run.mjs <base64 of the original>.' ADR-0008 Q5 / DECISIONS-r3 Q5: 'User permissions.deny also checks ctx_execute / ctx_execute_file / ctx_batch_execute input' — this list does not include the run.mjs wrapper, and the parser that unwraps sudo/env/bash -c/$() (ADR-0008 Q5) cannot see through a base64 blob to recover the original argv. So a user who added a permissions.deny rule to block a specific command or path never gets a second chance to block it once it is base64-wrapped and re-run.
findings.regression_risk: A user-authored permissions.deny rule (the exact mechanism ADR-0017 R4 promises to keep working: 'user hook timeouts, user hooks, permissions.deny, MCP entries they added: kept and reported, never removed') is silently defeated for every command that goes through Case B. This is worse than a missing feature — it is a deny rule that visibly exists in the user's config but stops matching.
findings.fix: Either (a) have the PreToolUse hook decode the base64 payload of run.mjs calls and re-run the full deny pipeline (shell parser + user permissions.deny) against the decoded command before allowing the wrapper, or (b) keep the deny decision attached to the wrapper invocation itself (deny it again, with the same reason) so a user-blocked command can never reach exec even through the rewritten path. Add a GP3/LV9 case: a subagent with `tools: Bash` and a user permissions.deny rule for `rm -rf /` must still be blocked when the same command is wrapped into run.mjs.

findings.title: Release skill runs `npm ci` on a dependency tree with no lockfile-integrity or audit gate before any release build step
findings.claim: Step 2 of the release skill is `npm ci && npm run build && node --test e2e/cases`, run on the `v2` branch before the release.yml build/publish jobs that produce the artifact users install from git.
findings.evidence: SKILL.md step 2 text: 'Run the deterministic tests: npm ci && npm run build && node --test e2e/cases.' ADR-0013's own `build` job explicitly strips npm entirely for the shipped artifact ('bundles, every manifest generated from adapters/table.ts, 3 skills, no package.json'), and `weekly.yml` runs `npm audit` only on a schedule, not on the release path. So the one step that actually compiles the bundle that `build`/`publish` later package runs through a full npm dependency resolution with no audit or lockfile-hash check gating it, on every single `/release` invocation.
findings.regression_risk: A compromised or typo-squatted dev dependency pulled by `npm ci` at build time can inject code into the bundle before the no-npm, checksum-signed `release` branch step ever runs — the SHA256SUMS/attestation in ADR-0013's build job authenticates the output of a step that itself had no supply-chain gate.
findings.fix: Either run `npm audit --audit-level=high` (or an equivalent lockfile-hash check against a committed known-good hash) as part of SKILL.md step 2, failing the release on drift, or state explicitly in ADR-0013 why the dev-time npm install is considered out of the release's trust boundary.

findings.title: ADR-0008's new `allowHosts` policy file for WebFetch has no v1 precedent, no schema, and no stated validation against SSRF-class hosts
findings.claim: Row 6 of the 'What changes' table: WebFetch denial is replaced by 'A host table that is never denied (the claude.ai artifact hosts). A user policy file with an allowHosts list.'
findings.evidence: git log -S"allowHosts" --all in cm-main returns zero commits — this is new v2 scope with no v1 implementation to inherit hardening from. The ADR gives no schema (wildcard rules? exact host match? scheme required?) and does not say whether an entry in allowHosts is still passed through the SSRF/redirect check that TECH-SPEC §SSRF (Q19) requires for ctx_fetch_and_index, or bypasses it entirely because the user explicitly allowed the host.
findings.regression_risk: If `allowHosts` bypasses the SSRF/redirect/private-IP check instead of just bypassing the deny-by-default, a user who adds an internal hostname (e.g. an internal wiki) to allowHosts for legitimate reasons reopens the exact DNS-rebinding/redirect-to-metadata gap the SSRF check exists to close, because the host entry is attacker-controllable by a later redirect once the first hop is allowed.
findings.fix: State explicitly: allowHosts only lifts the deny-by-default decision; the SSRF/private-IP/redirect-hop check (DECISIONS-r3 Q19, already flagged in REVIEW-r4a #8/#52) still runs on every hop even for allowlisted hosts. Add a GP3 case: an allowlisted host that 302-redirects to 169.254.169.254 must still be denied.

findings.title: ADR-0014's typed-key redaction scanner has no stated fallback when a secret appears inside a value that otherwise matches a safe type (e.g. hex40, semver)
findings.claim: Section 3 says every value passes a typed scanner (int, semver, hex40, date, enum, bool, JSON pointer); a value that fails becomes `<invalid>` and is dropped whole.
findings.evidence: The scanner classifies by shape, not by content review. A 40-character secret token that happens to look like a git `hex40` commit SHA (same character class, same length) would pass the hex40 check and be emitted verbatim, since the scanner does not distinguish 'is shaped like a commit sha' from 'is a commit sha'. REVIEW-r4a #43 already flags that the redaction allowlist was never diffed against v1's key list; this finding is narrower and still open: it is about the type-shape check itself admitting secret-shaped-like-hex40 values, independent of key-name allowlisting.
findings.regression_risk: Low likelihood (requires a secret format colliding with hex40/semver), but the report is explicitly sent by an AI agent to a public issue per the owner's Q18 'maximum debug data' rule, so any leak is public and unredactable after the fact.
findings.fix: For the hex40 field specifically, cross-check the value against a known commit range (e.g. `git cat-file -e`) before accepting it as a commit SHA rather than accepting any 40-hex-char string; or source hex40 fields only from values the server itself computed (e.g. `git rev-parse HEAD`), never from free-form input.
